newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh brake on credit may hurt stocks.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh brake on credit may hurt stocks.

text.p: Bangladesh's central bank has asked commercial banks to stop offering credit against securities to curb ballooning share prices and improve banks' liquidity positions, but brokers say the move may hurt the market.
Officials with commercial banks said on Monday the Bangladesh (central) Bank had instructed them to stop lending against securities as collateral.
The central bank in late 1994 allowed commercial banks to offer credit at a rate of 40 percent of the market value of shares for up to one million taka ($23,600).
The curb has been introduced to check a sharp rise in share prices -- surging since the June election victory of Sheikh Hasina -- and a liquidity shortfall for banks.
"This means the offering of credit against shares will be stopped," said one official.
Brokers said there would be little immediate impact on a market where capitalisation has almost doubled in a month, to $5.59 billion on Sunday from $2.84 billion on October 2.
It stood at $452 million at the end of 1994.
"The move is unlikely to have an immediate effect on the market as retail investors have enough funds in their hands," said broker Mostaque Ahmed.
"But in the long run the volume of trade will come down. I think this is a negative attitude of the central bank."

In a move to restrict credit expansion and increase mobilisation of savings, the central bank last week raised bank rates to 7.0 percent from 6.5 percent. It also hiked minimum interest rates on savings deposits and fixed deposits.
Bangladesh's stock market has been boosted by government steps including the lifting of restrictions on overseas investors trading initial public offerings (IPOs).
Moves to privatise public companies, offer foreign investors an exclusive industrial zone, and private investment in power and telecommunications has also boosted sentiment.
Bank officials defended their latest move, saying any brake on lending against shares would have little impact.
"Hundreds of retail investors now have enough funds to carry on their business. They have mostly mobilised their funds through selling land," said one official.
The officials said commercial banks had given some 500 million taka ($11.75 million) in loans to share traders.
Lutfar Rahman Sarkar, managing director of Prime Bank Ltd, said the diversion of funds from banks to the share market had squeezed other business activities.

"This may not be good either for the banking sector or the economy. Besides, the buoyancy in the share market has no relation to economic development in the country," the Financial Express newspaper on Friday quoted him as saying.
But others were critical of the move, saying it ran counter to the government's policy of boosting the capital market.
"The need of the time is to increase the volume of securities in the share-hungry market," former Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) chairman Khurshid Alam said.

Brokers on Monday said share prices continued to rise sharply. The benchmark DSE index reached an all-time high at 3,352.1 on Sunday. It was 2,986.29 on Thursday before the market closed for the Moslem Friday weekend.
